take: US refinery utilisation averaging above 95% between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998, is the key crude-to-products signal, implying strong run rates that underpin crude demand whilst keeping product cracks honest into the winter. The second theme is freight and macro: the global shipbuilding orderbook has surpassed its 2008 peak with Chinese yards tightening their grip, and LNG shipping is being reshaped by the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, both of which extend tonne-miles and support bunker demand even as dual-fuel container and vehicle carrier fleets pass 500 vessels. On flows, China’s rising crude imports are reducing its need to draw from its 1.3-billion-barrel strategic stash, a shift that removes a latent source of marginal demand and bears watching for spot crude balances. The cross-market link sits in Europe’s carbon market, where proposed shipping subsidies could make BioLNG cheaper than fuel oil, tilting the bunker complex away from residual fuel oil and into gas-derived alternatives. Watch in the next 24 hours for any escalation in the Iran attacks that have pushed oil into overbought territory for the third time this week, and for confirmation of Chinese import momentum against the inventory drawdown story.
